text: 3.1 Existing Methods
Elections today are run in three main ways, each with strengths and weaknesses.

items: **Paper ballots.** Trust comes from physical observation. They are transparent to those present at the booth and the count, but are slow, costly, hard for absent voters and open to local tampering.
**Electronic voting machines.** They are fast and widely used, but voters and observers cannot inspect the software inside, and an independent recount is limited to the machine's own record.
**Online voting through a central server.** It is convenient, but the server operator can in principle change or read votes, and a single attack on the server can affect the whole election.

**Earlier blockchain prototypes.** They remove the central record keeper but, as shown in Section 1.1, often leave identity linked to the vote, give one party the decryption key, or enforce rules in the web server.

text: 3.2 Proposed Method
The proposed system divides the trust so that no single component or person can break the secrecy or the integrity of the election alone.

items: The **backend server** knows who is on the electoral roll and who has voted. It produces a random token and an encrypted ballot, and it keeps no record that joins a voter to a ballot.
The **blockchain contract** holds the encrypted ballots and enforces the rules. It cannot read a vote, and it knows nothing about voters' identities.
The **trustees** can decrypt, but only together (two of three), and only after the election has closed.
The **public** can verify everything: the ballots on the chain, the published key and the tally.

text: Two ideas keep the identity and the ballot apart. First, the voter is known to the backend only by a hash, so the electoral roll holds no raw identities. Second, when the voter is verified the backend issues a random single-use token. The database stores only the hash of the token, and the table that holds tokens has no voter column and no timestamp, so even someone who reads the whole database cannot link a token to the person it was given to.

The user experience is deliberately simple. The voter sees one page and presses one button. All of the checking, hashing, encryption and blockchain work is done by the backend, step by step, and each step is timed and reported back to the page so that the process can be shown and explained.
3.3 System Overview, Block Diagram and Flow Chart

Figure 3.1 shows the block diagram. The voter's browser talks to a cloud server over HTTPS. Inside the server, Caddy receives the request and passes it to the backend, a Node.js program running in a Docker container, which keeps its records in a small SQLite database. The backend sends the encrypted ballot to the smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain. Three other parties stay outside the server: the administrator, who opens the election from their own wallet; the trustees, who hold the key shares; and the public, who can read and recount the ballots.

text: 3.4 Main Components
3.4.1 The voting page

The voting page is a single web page served by the backend. It lists a few dummy voter IDs (five fake citizens, of whom four are on the electoral roll) and one Vote button for each candidate. When a button is pressed, the page sends the voter ID and the candidate number to the backend. The answer lists the five steps with what each did and how long it took, and a receipt: a confirmation code (the token hash), the transaction hash and the block number on the chain. The fifth fake voter is deliberately not on the roll, so that a refusal can be shown.
3.4.2 Voter verification with a voter hash

The backend never stores a voter's identity. It calculates the voter hash as Keccak-256(HMAC-SHA-256(secret, "voter:" + identity reference)) and looks that hash up on the electoral roll. The secret stops anyone from guessing identities by hashing every possible number. If the hash is not on the roll the vote is refused at step 2, and nothing further happens.
3.4.3 Single-use voting token

If the voter is on the roll and has not yet voted, the backend generates 32 random bytes as a token and stores only their Keccak-256 hash. The voter's record is flagged as token issued, so a second token is refused with the message that the voter has already voted. The token table has no voter column and no timestamp. The token hash then travels with the ballot to the contract, which accepts each token hash only once.
3.4.4 Ballot encryption

The ballot is encrypted with a hybrid scheme using the election's public key. The plaintext is 17 bytes: one byte for the candidate number and 16 random bytes, which make two votes for the same candidate look completely different. It is sealed with a fresh AES-256 key in Galois/Counter Mode, and that AES key is wrapped with the election's RSA-3072 public key using OAEP with SHA-256. The associated data "gov-evoting:v1:<chain id>:<contract address>" is authenticated with the ciphertext, so a ballot cannot be moved to another election. The result is always 430 bytes (Figure 3.5), whichever candidate is chosen, so the size of a ballot reveals nothing.

In the one-button demonstration the backend performs this encryption. The full voter application of the project performs it in the voter's own browser instead, so that even the server never sees the choice. The demonstration trades that property for simplicity, and the report says so wherever it matters (Sections 3.8 and 6.2).

caption: Figure 3.5: Structure of an encrypted ballot (430 bytes)

text: 3.4.5 Smart contract (GovElection)
The Solidity contract keeps the election. Its main rules are given below.

items: Phases: Setup, Voting, Closed and Finalized, moving forward only.

Only the backend's submitter account can call castBallot(tokenHash, ballot). Each token hash can be used once, a ballot may be at most 1,024 bytes, and the number of ballots cannot exceed the number of eligible voters.
The hash of the election key is stored when the contract is created and cannot be changed.
After the end time, anyone can call closeElection(); nobody can close it early.
Trustees call submitTally(); the result is finalised only when two trustees submit identical totals.
Every important step emits an event, so the full history is public.

text: 3.4.6 Backend server and database

The backend is written for Node.js 24 with the Express web framework. Its database is SQLite, which Node.js includes. The backend protects itself in several ways: the voting request is rate-limited, the web pages carry a strict Content Security Policy, and the server writes no access log, so it keeps no record of who connected when. Transactions to the blockchain are sent one at a time through a queue so that two quick votes never reuse the same transaction number. Reads of the election state are cached for three seconds to avoid needless requests to the chain.

The backend also handles failure carefully. If the contract rejects a ballot, for example because voting just closed, the token is released and the voter may try again. If the outcome is uncertain, for example a timeout while waiting for confirmation, the voter stays marked as voted, because the ballot might have been recorded and a second ballot must not be possible. The voter is told to check the ballot count.
3.4.7 Key ceremony and trustees

Before the election a key ceremony generates the RSA-3072 key pair. The private key is split by Shamir secret sharing into three shares, any two of which rebuild it. Each share is encrypted for its trustee with a passphrase of at least twelve characters, using scrypt (N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1) to derive the key and AES-256-GCM to protect the share, with the share's details bound in as authenticated data. Only the public key goes to the server, and its hash is placed in the contract. The plain private key is never saved to disk.
3.4.8 Tally and public verification

After the election closes, two trustees supply their shares and passphrases, the private key is rebuilt, and its hash is compared with the hash stored on the chain. Each ballot is decrypted; a ballot that cannot be decrypted, or that names a candidate who does not exist, is counted as invalid and never stops the count. The trustees submit the totals together with a tally hash. When two identical submissions arrive the contract finalises the result. The private key is then published, and the verify-tally tool lets anyone download the ballots from the chain, decrypt them and check that the totals match.
3.4.9 Cloud deployment

The backend is packaged so that it can run on a cloud server instead of the developer's laptop. The server used is a small virtual machine on the Oracle Cloud free tier running Ubuntu 24.04, reached at a free DuckDNS address.

items: **Docker.** The backend is built into a container image in two stages, so the final image holds no build tools. Heavy development packages such as Hardhat are left out so that the build fits in the 1 GB memory of the small server. Two gigabytes of swap space are added to be safe.

**Caddy.** A second container, Caddy, faces the internet on ports 80 and 443. It obtains a free HTTPS certificate automatically for the server's public address and passes requests on to the backend. The public address is a free DuckDNS name.
**Persistent data.** The database lives on a Docker volume. If it were lost, voters could be issued a second token, so it must survive restarts.

**Blockchain connection.** The backend talks to the Sepolia test network through a remote procedure call (RPC) address. The contract is deployed with the administrator's wallet, and the wallets are funded with free test ether from a faucet.

**Deployment bundle.** A script prepares a folder containing only what the server needs: the settings file, the public election key, the compiled contract and the Docker files. The script checks that no wallet file and no trustee share is inside the folder.

**What stays off the server.** The server holds the backend's own submitter key, which can only submit ballots. The administrator's wallet and the trustees' shares stay with their owners, so a stolen server cannot read the votes or change the rules.

text: 3.5 Workflow of the System
The whole demonstration election follows the steps below. Table 3.1 gives the commands of the project that carry them out.

items: **Key ceremony.** The RSA-3072 key is generated and split into three trustee shares.
**Deployment.** The GovElection contract is deployed with the candidates, the trustees, the backend's submitter account, the voter limit and the hash of the election key.
**Server start.** The backend starts on the cloud server (or locally) and creates the demo voter list, in which four of five voters are on the roll.
**Opening.** The administrator opens the election for a fixed time window.
**Voting.** Each voter presses a Vote button; the five backend steps run; the voter sees a receipt.
**Closing.** When the end time passes, anyone can close the election.
**Tally.** Two trustees rebuild the key, decrypt, and submit identical totals; the contract finalises the result.
**Verification.** The key is published, and anyone can recount.

text: 3.6 Design Constraints

caption: Table 3.2: Design constraints and how they were handled
rows: Anonymity
Voter known only by a keyed hash; token table has no voter column or timestamp; fixed-size ballots; no access log.
Integrity
Rules enforced by the smart contract; ballots permanent on the chain; key hash fixed at deployment.
Eligibility
Electoral roll check on the voter hash; one token per voter; one ballot per token.
Distributed trust
2-of-3 threshold for decryption and for the tally.
Cost
Ballot kept at 430 bytes; about 417,000 gas per vote on the local chain and about 1.81 million on Sepolia (Section 5.1).
Speed
Whole pipeline about 0.23 s per vote on a laptop.
Usability
One page and one button; no wallet or cryptography knowledge needed by the voter.
Small server
Two-stage Docker build; development packages left out; swap space added; chain reads cached.
Secrets
Wallet keys and trustee shares never copied to the server; bundle checked automatically.
Time and budget
Free tools only; local test chain; free test network and free cloud tier for deployment.

text: 3.7 Engineering Standards and Guidelines

caption: Table 3.3: Standards and guidelines followed
rows: NIST SP 800-38D [9]
AES-GCM authenticated encryption of the ballot and of the key shares
RSA-OAEP wrapping of the AES key
HMAC for the voter hash
FIPS 180-4 [18] and FIPS 202 [20]
SHA-256 inside the HMAC and the key hash; Keccak-256 (the algorithm behind SHA-3) for voter and token hashes
Shamir secret sharing [8]
Threshold splitting of the election private key
OWASP Top 10 [23]
Input validation, rate limiting, safe error messages, no secrets in logs
W3C Content Security Policy [24]
Strict policy on the web pages to limit script injection
Aadhaar Act 2016 [19] and DPDP Act 2023 [21]
Minimal personal data; identity not stored in raw form
Solidity 0.8.x checked arithmetic
Overflow is rejected by the compiler

text: 3.8 Threat Model

Table 3.4 lists the attacks considered and the defence against each. Most of the defences are covered by automated tests; the last two rows are design properties checked by reasoning and by the deployment bundle's secret check.

caption: Table 3.4: Threats and defences
rows: Voting twice
One token per voter in the database, and one ballot per token hash in the contract.
Reading the votes
Hybrid encryption; the private key is split 2-of-3 among trustees and appears only after voting closes.
Administrator reading or changing votes
The administrator never holds the key, and the contract gives that role no access to ballots.
Fake ballots
Only the backend's submitter account can submit, and the ballot count is capped at the voter limit.
Replaying a ballot in another election
The chain number and contract address are bound into the encryption, so a copy fails to decrypt.
Changing a stored ballot
AES-GCM detects any change, and the blockchain is append-only.
Stolen database
Only keyed hashes are stored: no identity and no vote.
Stolen cloud server
The server holds only the public key and the submitter key; it cannot decrypt or change the rules.
A wrong count
Two trustees must submit identical totals, and anyone can recount the public ballots.
Flooding and guessing
Rate limits and a strict content security policy.
Server links a voter to a ballot

Not fully prevented in the demonstration. In the one-button page the backend sees the voter and the choice in one request and encrypts it itself. The database holds no link, but a dishonest server could keep one. The full application encrypts in the browser; stronger protection needs zero-knowledge proofs (Section 6.3).
